rows.summary: Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. Your own order system shows the tote was never shipped because it was out of stock, so there is no delivery evidence to contest with. Refunding now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. The only tracking on file shows CANCELLED, not delivered, so there is no proof of delivery to contest this item-not-received case, and settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation.

Message the buyer with the tracking number and explain the tote has shipped and is on its way. Tracking shows only SHIPPED, not delivered, so contesting now would not persuade PayPal, and refunding is premature two days after payment.

Message the buyer first. They opened the case the day before the USPS scan you entered shows delivery to their ZIP code, so the tote has probably arrived since. PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED, so ask the buyer to check and close the case. If they don't, submit proof of delivery.

You've already submitted tracking and offered a $20 refund, and PayPal is waiting on the buyer, so send a short follow-up and wait. PayPal's tracker shows only SHIPPED, not delivered, so if the buyer still reports nothing arrived, a fair offer or refund is likely cheaper than escalation.

Refund the full $120.00. The delivery scan you entered doesn't match the buyer's address (ZIP 10001 vs 95131), and PayPal's own tracker shows only 'Shipped,' so contesting is unlikely to succeed. Resolving now avoids escalation and the dispute fee. Before accepting, check the tracking number on USPS's own site. Contest only if USPS clearly shows delivery to 95131.

Refund the $48.00 in full. The only delivery scan is dated Sep 28, four days before the buyer paid on Oct 2, so it can't be this order's delivery. PayPal's tracker also shows only SHIPPED, which wouldn't win a not-received case. If you find a correct tracking number showing delivery to the San Jose address after Oct 2, contest with that instead.

Submit supporting info to PayPal showing USPS delivered the tote to the buyer's shipping ZIP, along with the tracking number already on the order. The delivery scan was entered by you, so attach the official USPS tracking record to back it up.

Accept the claim and refund the $48.00. The only tracking on file is cancelled, so you have no proof of delivery to win this item-not-received chargeback, and PayPal does not allow a partial offer at this stage.

PayPal currently allows no actions on this $48.00 item-not-received chargeback while it is under review, so there is nothing to do in PayPal right now. Outside PayPal, gather any carrier tracking showing delivery to the San Jose address, since no tracking is on file and it would be the key evidence if PayPal asks for a response.

Refund the $8.00 in full. There is no tracking to prove delivery, so contesting would likely fail, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee. Also note that your order record lists a vinyl sticker while PayPal lists a canvas tote, so check that you matched the right order.

Don't refund. The buyer says they found the tote at a neighbor's and will close the case, so reply politely and ask them to close it on PayPal. Your tracking shows only 'shipped', not delivered, so it isn't strong enough to contest right now.

Message the buyer now: the merchant's notes show a signed UPS delivery, but PayPal's tracker only shows the package as shipped. Before contesting this $900 case, get the official UPS proof of delivery and confirm it matches the tracking number on the order.

Refund the buyer the full 300.00 USD. There is no tracking or proof of shipment on file and the transaction isn't covered by seller protection, so contesting would likely fail, and settling during the inquiry avoids PayPal's dispute fee. If you do have carrier tracking showing delivery to the San Jose address, submit that as evidence instead.

Message the buyer with the tracking number and offer to help locate the tote; messaging is the only action PayPal allows right now. Tracking shows the package as shipped but not delivered, which would not be strong enough to contest.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The buyer confirms tracking shows delivered, the carrier scan shows delivery to the order's ZIP code, and the sale qualifies for seller protection. Before submitting, check the tracking number on USPS.com and attach the official USPS delivery record, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you.

Submit proof of delivery: the USPS scan shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 4, and the buyer has already rejected your $15 offer. Attach the official USPS tracking record, since the delivery scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Refund the full 30.00 USD now. The buyer reports and photographs a broken mug, you have no evidence on file to rebut it, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids an escalated claim and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer first. Your listing says olive green and your Oct 2 packing photo shows an olive green tote, but color perception is subjective, so a friendly message offering to share the photo and discuss options may resolve this inquiry before it escalates and incurs a dispute fee.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. USPS shows delivery to the buyer's San Jose ZIP, and the packed and label weight of 1.8 lb argues against an empty box. Strengthen the case by making sure the PayPal tracker shows Delivered rather than only your own scan entry.

Offer a $25.00 partial refund for the missing tote. Your own packing log confirms only 1 of the 2 ordered totes was packed, so contesting would fail, and settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer before taking any other step. Their complaint is a single unexplained line, and you hold an authenticity certificate matching serial MX-22841. Share it, ask what makes them think the tote is fake, and hold off on refunding or contesting until you understand the concern.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The sale is eligible for seller protection, and USPS tracking shows delivery to the ship-to address on the order, which is what PayPal looks for in an unauthorized-transaction claim. Attach the USPS delivery confirmation; PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED, and the delivery scan was entered by you.

Refund the $15.00 in full. This is an unauthorized-payment case on a digital download that isn't covered by seller protection, so contesting is unlikely to win, and settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and a possible dispute fee.
Submit proof of refund: your log shows a full 48.00 USD refund (ID 6RT43210AB987654C) was already issued via PayPal on 2026-10-03. Do not accept the claim, because that would refund the buyer twice.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. Your returns log shows a return was received but no refund was issued, so there is no proof of refund to contest with, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and its fee. First confirm that return #2290 belongs to this buyer's tote order.

Accept the claim and refund the 48.00 USD. Your own order system shows the buyer was charged twice for one shipped tote, so the duplicate-charge complaint is valid. Resolving now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and the dispute fee.

Submit proof of fulfillment: USPS tracking shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, and the sale is covered by seller protection. The buyer's message gives no real complaint, only an instruction to refund, so it should not drive your decision.

PayPal currently allows no actions on this item-not-received inquiry, so take no action in PayPal for now. Outside PayPal, find the carrier tracking for the tote shipped to the San Jose address; no delivery proof is on file yet, and you will need it if the case escalates.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The USPS scan shows the tote was delivered to the front door in the buyer's ZIP code, and the order is eligible for seller protection. Attach the official USPS tracking page, since the delivery scan on file was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Submit proof of delivery: USPS shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, the day after the buyer opened this not-received case. Attach the official USPS tracking record, because the delivery scan was entered by you and PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Message the buyer that USPS shows the tote delivered to their front door on Oct 4, the day after they wrote to you, and ask them to check and close the case. Hold off on contesting: the only delivery scan was entered by you, and PayPal's own tracker still shows SHIPPED, so confirm delivery on the USPS record before submitting proof of fulfillment.

Message the buyer before refunding: the order was a canvas tote, but the buyer's photo shows a cracked ceramic mug, so ask them to confirm the order and send photos of the tote and its packaging. We have no shipping or tracking evidence on file, so contesting now would be weak; if the buyer shows the tote really arrived damaged, a refund or offer is the fair next step.

Don't offer a refund for now: your tracking scan shows the tote delivered to the buyer's ZIP. PayPal only allows an offer at this stage. Confirm the USPS delivery on the carrier's site, consider contacting the buyer outside PayPal to say it was left at the front door, and submit the tracking as proof of fulfillment if the case escalates.

Don't contest yet: the tracking shows only SHIPPED, not delivered, so it won't win an item-not-received case. Message the buyer that you are checking with the carrier, and contact the carrier yourself. If the package isn't found or delivered soon, move to a full refund rather than escalating a $1,200 case without proof of delivery.
